milestone.title: Jack Tramiel abruptly leaves Commodore
milestone.note: The departure ended the leadership era that made the VIC-20 and Commodore 64 mass-market machines and would soon reshape both Commodore and Atari.

editorNote: EXTRA: Commodore’s founder departs just as the home-computer price war reaches a decisive turn.
morningLine: The billion-dollar home-computer giant awakens without the man who built its low-price empire.

lead.headline: TRAMIEL QUITS COMMODORE
lead.dek: Founder’s surprise Friday resignation, days after his CES appearance, leaves the company’s next generation under a cloud.
body: Jack Tramiel resigned as president and chief executive of Commodore International on Friday, January 13, an abrupt break at the company he had driven from office-machine roots into the center of the home-computer boom. The news followed only days after Tramiel personally championed Commodore’s new 264 family at the Winter Consumer Electronics Show.

The timing makes the departure more than an executive shuffle. Commodore’s VIC-20 and Commodore 64 had turned price into a weapon, putting capable color computers into mass-market stores and forcing every rival to answer. COMPUTE! estimated that the company’s annual sales pace had multiplied roughly twenty-fivefold in six or seven years.

Tramiel said a billion-dollar company now required a “professional executive.” Marshall F. Smith, an industrial executive with manufacturing and finance experience but no computer-industry background, was expected to take charge in late February. Until then, dealers and developers must judge whether Commodore’s famously aggressive course will continue.

The unanswered question hangs over the 264 and speech-equipped 364V. Both promise 64K, an improved BASIC and built-in productivity tools, but sacrifice much of the Commodore 64’s game compatibility. The machines arrived as the industry’s shakeout became visible; now their most forceful sponsor has left the stage.

stories.headline: Games Trade Finds Guarded Relief at CES
body: After the bruising 1983 market collapse, the New York Times found a “sigh of relief” among video-game exhibitors on January 10. The confidence was cautious: companies were narrowing their lines, emphasizing proven machines and searching for ways to keep cartridge buyers interested.

Mattel Electronics had been sold to investors, yet its booth still showed a System Changer for Atari 2600 cartridges, new Intellivision games and Apple and IBM titles. Computer Entertainer’s January tally kept Miner 2049er, Ms. Pac-Man and River Raid among the period’s strongest sellers.

The show-floor message is survival through software and compatibility. The arcade spirit remains alive, but the extravagant hardware race has yielded to sharper bets on games people will actually buy.

stories.headline: Commodore’s 264 Family Promises an Office in ROM
body: The 264 and talking 364V pair 64K of memory with BASIC 3.5, whose disk, graphics, sound and structured-programming commands answer long-standing complaints about the Commodore 64’s sparse built-in language. More than 59K is available to BASIC.

Commodore’s proposed 3-Plus-1 package combines word processing, filing, spreadsheet work and business graphics. The 364V adds a numeric keypad and Magic Voice speech synthesis, aiming squarely at buyers who want an appliance rather than a hobby kit.

That convenience carries a cost: C64 cartridges, joysticks and Datasette gear do not transfer, and the TED chip lacks the C64’s sprites and celebrated SID sound. Commodore says the 264 will sell below $500, but has announced no firm price.

stories.headline: Coleco Builds an Adam Comeback Plan
body: Coleco answered Adam’s troubled debut with a large CES expansion plan: a floppy drive, modem, RAM card, second data drive, CP/M support and a pledge of 170 software packages. Honeywell had opened five service centers and planned thirty more.

Questions remain over reliability and price. Creative Computing cited published claims of high initial defect rates, which a Coleco spokesman rejected, while wholesale pricing rose about 20 percent to $650 and New York retail quotes reached $700 to $799.
The accessories could turn Adam into a broader computer system, but the comeback now depends on delivery, service and restoring buyer confidence.
